source.title_on_document: Rapid AIdeation: Generating Ideas With the Self and in Collaboration With Large Language Models

supplement.where: Appendix A, pp. 7-8 of the PDF

paper_design_summary: Twenty-one university students took part in a 40-minute online rapid-ideation workshop in random groups of three. Each person first brainstormed ideas alone (Self Ideation) and then with ChatGPT (Co-GPT Ideation), always in that order, on one of two issues (misinformation, hallucination). The authors counted unique idea clusters per phase and compared the post-its that groups picked as their top three ideas; there is no statistical test.

studies.label: Rapid ideation workshop (Self Ideation then Co-GPT Ideation)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Every participant did both phases in a fixed order: Self Ideation first, then Co-GPT Ideation. Only the groups of three were formed at random, and groups were assigned to one of two issues (random assignment of issues not stated).
assignment.quote: For the study, we only assessed Self Ideation ideation followed by Co-GPT Ideation ideation and a follow-up comparing with the reverse order will be important.
assignment.locator: p. 5, Section 6 Limitations; also p. 2, Section 3.1 and Figure 1

arms.name: Self Ideation
arms.description: Crazy 8's brainstorming alone, entering ideas as post-its on slides

arms.name: Co-GPT Ideation
arms.description: Same Crazy 8's activity, but participants used ChatGPT to generate ideas

participants.who: University students; of the 15 who answered the optional survey, 6 undergraduates, 6 master's and 3 doctoral students, all previously experienced with ChatGPT. Same 21 people in both phases (4 groups on misinformation, 3 on hallucination). The paper does not state that any participant was dropped; 17 of 21 voluntarily submitted ChatGPT conversations.
participants.quote: The study involved 21 participants from the student population at a university. Participation was voluntary with no compensation provided.
participants.locator: p. 3, Section 3.2 Participants; group counts p. 3, Section 4

ai_tool.how_used: Participants prompted ChatGPT freely to generate ideas for their group's issue and entered ideas as post-its; 59 prompts from 17 submitted conversations (p. 3, Section 4; model version p. 5, Section 6).

task.description: Rapid ideation (Crazy 8's) on 'ways to utilize ChatGPT to address online misinformation' or 'ways to address the hallucination issue of ChatGPT'
task.duration: 16 minutes for the two individual phases combined; 40-minute workshop (p. 2, Figure 1 and Section 3.1)

contrasts.reported: 23.6% more unique ideas with Co-GPT Ideation (Self Ideation: 38, Co-GPT Ideation: 47); Misinformation 21 vs 26; Hallucination 17 vs 21. Post-its: 108 (Self) vs 119 (Co-GPT). No test.

contrasts.reported: Top-three post-its: Self Ideation 9, Co-GPT Ideation 12 (Misinformation 5 vs 7; Hallucination 4 vs 5). Table 1 ranks First/Second/Third: Self 4/3/2, Co-GPT 3/4/5. No test.

outcomes.name: Character length of each group's top-three representative post-its
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Character counts of the top-three representative post-its selected by each group during Ranking (p. 4, Section 4.2). The paper does not state how characters were counted. The codebook provides no exact measure category for raw character counts, so measure is null. The reported means and SDs describe the selected post-its.

contrasts.reported: Top-three representative post-it length: Co-GPT Ideation M = 146.8, SD = 86.8 characters; Self Ideation M = 97.7, SD = 50.7 characters. Selected post-its: Co-GPT Ideation 12, Self Ideation 9. Descriptive statistics only; no test.
contrasts.locator: p. 4, Section 4.2; descriptive analysis specified on p. 3, Section 3.3

eligibility.reason: Within-person comparison with a fixed order (Self Ideation always before Co-GPT Ideation, p. 5, Section 6), so AI use was not randomly assigned; only group membership was random. Only 21 people took part (p. 3, Section 3.2), well below 50. Outcomes (unique-idea counts, groups' top-three picks) are scored on the output. Triage called it a small experiment; it is a non-randomized before-after comparison (quasi_people), which the codebook folds into observational context (Review 1 open question on whether such designs appear as context or only in the screening report).

one_line_finding: With ChatGPT the 21 students produced more unique idea clusters (47 vs 38 alone, p. 3, Section 4.1) and slightly more of their groups' top-three picks (12 vs 9, p. 4, Section 4.2 and Table 1), with no statistical test and a fixed condition order.
